node.label: Anthony Pagden
node.date_label: The Fall of Natural Man (1982) · European Encounters with the New World (1993) · Lords of All the World (1995)
node.description: An intellectual historian of empire and international political ideas. His interview connects European self-understanding to overseas encounters and distinguishes the modern project of European union from an empire, while stating his own cosmopolitan and progress-oriented commitments.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Fall of Natural Man (1982); European Encounters with the New World (1993); Lords of All the World (1995).
node.scope_note: Selected substantive passages and bibliographic records only; complete monographs not read. Existing profile/field prose, collective relationships and earlier verification qualifications remain unchanged. Citation counts selected the research queue; they do not prove importance or influence. Life status is separately documented in this local person folder; no lifespan or career interval is inferred.

incident_edges.relationship: Studies European political self-understanding through ideas of empire and relations with peoples outside Europe.

incident_edges.relationship: Connects projects of European unity with imperial experience and changing international arrangements.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes Europe’s aggregate of states from empire, while acknowledging imperial preservation as part of the history. His cosmopolitan-progressive evaluation remains his position.

incident_edges.relationship: Dickason questions Pagden’s account of rejected imperial doctrines by distinguishing theoretical argument from their continued use in practical colonial policy (1997).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Review of Lords of All the World, especially its treatment of Hostiensis and Edward Coke. She also praises the book’s contribution to comparative colonial studies; this is not rejection of the whole project. The review’s original heading prints Worlds, whereas the identified 1995 book title uses World. Full review read; Pagden’s book body remains unread.

strands.focus: Duara frames national, local and transnational histories as potentially conflicting rather than one evolutionary story.

strands.title: Comparison and connection in dispute
strands.focus: Lieberman’s state comparisons and Subrahmanyam’s circulation are interlocutory projects, not successive universal methods.

strands.title: Reciprocal comparison and connected units
strands.focus: Pomeranz names Wong’s reciprocal comparison and Tilly’s encompassing comparison as resources. Regions, states and wider systems answer different questions; the method does not require treating Europe and China as internally uniform.

strands.title: Proto-industry and the limits of trade
strands.focus: Pomeranz extends Mokyr’s labor model across regions while questioning unlimited manufacture exports and resource imports at unchanged relative prices. Comparing regions also requires examining their trading partners.

strands.title: Legal ordering across empires
strands.focus: Benton uses jurisdictional conflicts to ask how local cultural practices formed repeated institutional patterns across empires. This strategy places legal ordering alongside other ways of relating local encounters to global structures. Her 2002 introduction is read; the 2013 volume with Richard J. Ross and Stern’s separate 2011 corporate-sovereignty book are bibliographic resources, not evidence of a single school or transmission.
strands.works: Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint); Benton and Ross, eds., Legal Pluralism and Empires (2013, body unread). Further comparative resource: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011, publisher metadata only).

strands.title: Capitalism as connected regional diversity
strands.focus: In his 2020 methodological answer Beckert relates regional differences and connections: merchants, plantations, manufacturing and state power belong in the same global inquiry. His account resists treating Europe’s industrialisation as the whole history of capitalism. This strand records his stated strategy; the empirical adequacy of its global applications and criticism of the cotton argument remain open.
strands.works: GrowthPolicy interview with Devjani Roy (2020), answer 2; Empire of Cotton (2014, existing limited excerpt)

neighbor_nodes.label: Intellectual history
neighbor_nodes.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
neighbor_nodes.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Arthur O. Lovejoy: The Great Chain of Being (1936); Quentin Skinner: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); J. G. A. Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.
